{{Short description|Tauberian theorem}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem''' is a [[Tauberian theorem]] relating the [[asymptotics]] of the partial sums of a [[series (mathematics)|series]] with the asymptotics of its [[Abel summation]]. In this form, the theorem asserts that if the sequence
<math>a_n\geq 0</math> is such that there is an [[asymptotic equivalence]]
:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n e^{-ny} \sim \frac{1}{y}\ \text{as}\ y\downarrow 0</math>
then there is also an asymptotic equivalence
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^n a_k \sim n</math>
as <math>n\to\infty</math>.  The [[integral]] formulation of the theorem relates in an analogous manner the asymptotics of the [[cumulative distribution function]] of a function with the asymptotics of its [[Laplace transform]].

The theorem was [[mathematical proof|proved]] in 1914 by [[G. H. Hardy]] and [[J. E. Littlewood]].<ref name=Titchmarsh>
{{cite book |last1=Titchmarsh |first1=E. C. |authorlink1=Edward Charles Titchmarsh |title=The Theory of Functions |url=https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.2588 |edition=2nd |year=1939 |publisher=Oxford University Press |location=Oxford |isbn=0-19-853349-7}}
</ref>{{Rp|226}} In 1930, [[Jovan Karamata]] gave a new and much simpler proof.<ref name=Titchmarsh />{{Rp|226}}

==Statement of the theorem==

===Series formulation===
This formulation is from Titchmarsh.<ref name=Titchmarsh />{{Rp|226}} Suppose <math>a_n\geq 0</math> for all <math>n\in\mathbb{N}</math>, and we have
:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n x^n \sim \frac{1}{1-x}\ \text{as}\ x\uparrow 1 .</math>
Then as <math>n\to\infty</math> we have
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^n a_k \sim n.</math>
The theorem is sometimes quoted in equivalent forms, where instead of requiring <math>a_n\geq 0</math>, we require <math>a_n=O(1)</math>, or we require 
<math>a_n\geq -K</math> for some constant <math>K</math>.<ref name=Hardy>
{{cite book |last1=Hardy |first1=G. H. |authorlink1=G. H. Hardy |title=Divergent Series |year=1991 |orig-date=1949 |publisher=AMS Chelsea |location=Providence, RI |isbn=0-8284-0334-1}}
</ref>{{Rp|155}} The theorem is sometimes quoted in another equivalent formulation (through the change of variable <math>x=1/e^y</math>).<ref name=Hardy />{{Rp|155}} 
If,
:<math>\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_n e^{-ny} \sim \frac{1}{y}\ \text{as}\ y\downarrow 0 </math>
then
:<math>\sum_{k=0}^n a_k \sim n.</math>

===Integral formulation===
The following more general formulation is from Feller.<ref>{{Cite book | last1=Feller | first1=William | author1-link=William Feller | title=An introduction to probability theory and its applications. Vol. II. | publisher=[[John Wiley & Sons]] | location=New York | series=Second edition |mr=0270403 | year=1971}}
</ref>{{Rp|445}} Consider a [[real number|real]]-valued function <math>F:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}</math> of [[bounded variation]].<ref>Bounded variation is only required locally: on every bounded subinterval of <math>[0,\infty)</math>.  However, then more complicated additional assumptions on the convergence of the Laplace–Stieltjes transform are required. See {{Cite book | last1=Shubin | first1=M. A. | title=Pseudodifferential operators and spectral theory | publisher=[[Springer-Verlag]] | location=Berlin, New York | series=Springer Series in Soviet Mathematics | isbn=978-3-540-13621-7 |mr=883081 | year=1987}}</ref>  The [[Laplace–Stieltjes transform]] of <math>F</math> is defined by the [[Stieltjes integral]]

:<math>\omega(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}\,dF(t).</math>

The theorem relates the asymptotics of ω with those of <math>F</math> in the following way. If <math>\rho</math> is a non-negative real number, then the following statements are equivalent
*<math>\omega(s)\sim C s^{-\rho},\quad\rm{as\ }s\to 0</math>
*<math>F(t)\sim \frac{C}{\Gamma(\rho+1)}t^\rho, \ \text{as}\ t\to\infty.</math>
Here <math>\Gamma</math> denotes the [[Gamma function]]. One obtains the theorem for series as a special case by taking <math>\rho=1</math> and <math>F(t)</math> to be a piecewise constant function with value <math>\textstyle{\sum_{k=0}^n a_k}</math> between <math>t=n</math> and <math>t=n+1</math>.

A slight improvement is possible. According to the definition of a [[slowly varying function]], <math>L(x)</math> is slow varying at infinity iff
:<math>\frac{L(tx)}{L(x)}\to 1,\quad x\to\infty</math>
for every <math>t>0</math>. Let <math>L</math> be a function slowly varying at infinity and <math>\rho\geq 0</math>. Then the following statements are equivalent
*<math>\omega(s)\sim s^{-\rho}L(s^{-1}),\quad\text{as}\ s\to 0</math>
*<math>F(t)\sim \frac{1}{\Gamma(\rho+1)}t^\rho L(t), \quad\text{as}\ t\to\infty.</math>

==Karamata's proof==

{{harvtxt|Karamata|1930}} found a short proof of the theorem by considering the functions <math>g</math> such that
:<math>\lim_{x\to 1} (1-x)\sum a_nx^ng(x^n) = \int_0^1 g(t)dt</math>
An easy calculation shows that all [[monomial]]s <math>g(x)=x^k</math> have this property, and therefore so do all [[polynomial]]s <math>g</math>. This can be extended to a function <math>g</math> with simple (step) [[discontinuity (mathematics)|discontinuities]] by approximating it by polynomials from above and below (using the [[Weierstrass approximation theorem]] and a little extra fudging) and using the fact that the coefficients <math>a_n</math> are positive. In particular the function given by <math>g(t)=1/t</math> if <math>1/e<t<1</math> and <math>0</math> otherwise has this property. But then for <math>x=e^{-1/N}</math> the sum 
<math>\sum a_n x^n g(x^n)</math> is <math>a_0 + \cdots + a_N</math> and the integral of <math>g</math> is <math>1</math>, from which the Hardy–Littlewood theorem follows immediately.

==Examples==

===Non-positive coefficients===

The theorem can fail without the condition that the coefficients are non-negative. For example, the function
:<math>\frac{1}{(1+x)^2(1-x)} = 1-x+2x^2-2x^3+3x^4-3x^5+\cdots</math>
is asymptotic to <math>1/4(1-x)</math> as <math>x\to 1</math>, but the partial sums of its coefficients are 1, 0, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4, ... and are not asymptotic to any linear function.

===Littlewood's extension of Tauber's theorem===

{{main|Littlewood's Tauberian theorem}}
In 1911 [[John Edensor Littlewood|Littlewood]] proved an extension of [[Alfred Tauber|Tauber]]'s [[converse (logic)|converse]] of [[Abel's theorem]]. Littlewood showed the following: If <math>a_n=O(1/n)</math>, and we have 
:<math>\sum a_n x^n \to s \ \text{as}\ x\uparrow 1 </math>
then
:<math> \sum a_n = s.</math>
This came historically before the Hardy–Littlewood Tauberian theorem, but can be proved as a simple application of it.<ref name=Titchmarsh />{{Rp|233–235}}

===Prime number theorem===
In 1915 Hardy and Littlewood developed a proof of the [[prime number theorem]] based on their Tauberian theorem; they proved
:<math>\sum_{n=2}^\infty \Lambda(n) e^{-ny} \sim \frac{1}{y},</math>
where <math>\Lambda</math> is the [[von Mangoldt function]], and then conclude
:<math> \sum_{n \le x} \Lambda(n) \sim x,</math>
an equivalent form of the prime number theorem.<ref name=12Ramanujan>
{{cite book | last = Hardy | first = G. H. |authorlink=G. H. Hardy | title = Ramanujan: Twelve Lectures on Subjects Suggested by his Life and Work | publisher = AMS Chelsea Publishing | location = Providence | year = 1999 |orig-date=1940 | isbn = 978-0-8218-2023-0 }}</ref>{{Rp|34–35}}<ref name=Narkiewicz>
{{cite book | last = Narkiewicz | first = Władysław | title = The Development of Prime Number Theory | publisher = Springer-Verlag | location = Berlin | year = 2000 | isbn = 3-540-66289-8 }}
</ref>{{Rp|302–307}}
Littlewood developed a simpler proof, still based on this Tauberian theorem, in 1971.<ref name=Narkiewicz />{{Rp|307–309}}
